HEADLINE: A Christmas carol
INTRO: I've been waking from particularly vivid dreams the past few days - must be all the Sakata rice crackers and vacuum-sealed cabanossi in my system. These dreams have been of Christmases past.
TEXT:
I've been waking from particularly vivid dreams the past few days - must be all the Sakata rice crackers and vacuum-sealed cabanossi in my system. These dreams have been of Christmases past.

The first Christmas I remember was in our dilapidated farmhouse at the end of an unsealed road in central west NSW. It is cool and dark in the living room (notwithstanding the lights on the tree) and my little sister Madeline is resplendent in a terry towelling jumpsuit. I am given a puppy, a Jack Russell terrier, whom I christen Clark Kent (of course I named my first dog after a superhero who wears spectacles and writes for a newspaper). The little mutt has acres around which to roam, but instead parks himself directly outside my parents' bedroom window and yaps incessantly through the night. Before the week is out, Clark has decamped to the pound.

I dream of Tasmania, and the infinitude of those few hours before Christmas, the involuntary sleeplessness, and the harrowing hunger, of the overnight. Despite buzzing exhaustion, I listen excitedly for every creak and rustle. As day dawns down on the 42nd southern parallel, I sneak up the stairs and perch myself at their summit, desperate for a glimpse of what's landed beneath that same PVC tree, before I'm yelled at to return to bed.

I dream of Christmas in Yagoona, and cricket with my cousins on that downward slope out back, far, far hotter than I'm accustomed to, and more mozzies, sprinklers fizzing, and then my mottled, sweet-smelling grandfather pulls me aside to warn that he'll soon be dead, that I'll probably never see him again. Despite this festive premonition, Granddad lives another 15 years.

Christmas as a young adult isn't as much fun as I accounted for. Sure, you can do whatever you want, but everything is closed, you're dead broke and nobody is around. Remember, this is well before Facebook emerges to connect the city's orphans. Thanks to an infernal yacht race and a dubiously commendable food festival, it is cripplingly expensive to fly to Hobart, where the parentals still, at this point, reside (although Yule with them is hardly the exercise of emancipation). My sister ditches me for a barbecue in Bronte with her pinhead boyfriend and his tax-dodging surfie mates, which I will never entirely forgive her for. So in my Darlinghurst flat, I spend the day watching DVDs and calling around in an ultimately fruitless bid to muster up some company. Xanax then gets me through to Boxing Day.

Five years later (and five years ago now), I spend December 25 alone in the Middle East. My sister, again, and this time with my mother, decides to spend it without me, in nearby Oman. In their absence, I alternate between G&Ts and pinot grigio until I black out on the bathroom floor.

I've since learned to enjoy this strange festival, and its quietude - the shops are shut and the phone is eerily quiet, but otherwise it's just a normal day, and that's how I treat it. We spend all year yearning for a quiet moment, so why freak out when it presents itself?

All the Astons now live in NSW, which helps, but Mum's a midwife and my brother Lachy is a copper, and neither bad guys nor heavily pregnant women necessarily adhere to the public holiday schedule.

This year, Dad takes the train up from Nowra and joins me for lunch at Gowings, where we slog through a feast of raw seafood, turkey and pudding (not to mention plenty of champagne). I'm in bed by 6pm.

For I'm acutely aware that Christmas Day is merely Boxing Day Eve (a descriptor, I believe, originally conceived by Fairfax columnist Greg Baum). I wake and sit by the open window in the early sun, catching up on the best long reads of 2015 from The Guardian and The New Yorker and Condé Nast and The Daily Beast, and late as I am, fire up my favourite carols - O Magnum Mysterium and (incongruously) In the Bleak Midwinter, and Vaughan Williams' arrangement of The Truth Above. I watch the first episode of Narcos on Netflix and make myself an Aperol spritz, cut more of that cabanossi. And then the Melbourne rain subsides and another lopsided Test begins on Channel Nine, and Maddie and Dylan arrive carting fresh spaghetti and wine and disappear immediately into the kitchen, and this really isn't such a bad way for a couple of days to elapse, is it?

And next comes New Year's Eve, which, historically, I've been really bad at too. But that's a whole other story ... W

HEADLINE: Australia missing the boat in Asia boom
INTRO: Anyone needing a reminder of Australia's proximity to Asia did not have to look much further than a Sydney beach, a Tasmanian oyster farm or a Melbourne casino over the holiday period. There is evidence of the rapid growth of Chinese inbound tourism everywhere.
TEXT:
Anyone needing a reminder of Australia's proximity to Asia did not have to look much further than a Sydney beach, a Tasmanian oyster farm or a Melbourne casino over the holiday period. There is evidence of the rapid growth of Chinese inbound tourism everywhere.

But while airlines, hotels and tourism operators have been quick to jump on the Asian tourism boom, most Australian companies are still failing to capitalise on the opportunity of being on the doorstep of the world's fastest-growing economies.

It has been more than three years since Julia Gillard's Asian Century white paper outlined many of the issues holding back Australia in the region. That document, launched in a blaze of publicity, attempted to deliver a long-term blueprint for fixing the problem.

It is easy to forget it ever existed. Political upheaval meant many of the aspirational goals outlined in the document were brushed aside as the Abbott government secured important trade agreements with Japan, South Korea and China.

The creation of a new trade and investment zone in south-east Asia this weekend marks another milestone in efforts to break down trade barriers and enhance opportunities for Australian exporters in the region. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations Economic Community formally starts trading on January 1.

But that alone will not address the huge imbalance in the focus that the boards and management of Australian companies continue to give the region compared with Western markets, such as the United States, Europe and smaller neighbours like New Zealand.

While innovation was the buzzword of 2015, the lack of a comprehensive long-term plan for engaging in Asia remains a major challenge for the Turnbull government heading into 2016.

Cultural differences and short-termism are the two key reasons why corporate Australia is in danger of missing the boat in terms of Asia.

"It is a once in a lifetime opportunity but we have to act now. If we don't it will happen around us and we will be forever reacting to the situation rather than shaping that opportunity," says Andrew Parker, the head of PricewaterhouseCoopers' Asian practice in Australia.

Parker is talking about capitalising on the unprecedented growth of wealth on our doorstep, something that most companies outside of mining have ignored for the past decade.

Research published by Parker a year ago showed 9 per cent of Australian companies operated in Asia and only 23 per cent of large corporations had staff on the ground in the region. The most staggering find from the study was the 65 per cent who said they had no intention of changing their stance towards Asia in the next two to three years.

Parker says the statistics are relevant a year later. Those statistics were based on 2013 Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) data. The latest available data for 2014 showed nothing has changed. Australia's investment in New Zealand went from $47.4 billion in 2013 to $61.6 billion in 2014. Investment in China increased less than $1 billion from $11.4 billion to $12.1 billion. The United States was the top destination for Australian investment abroad, accounting for 25 per cent at $136.2 billion.

"Trade agreements are fantastic but they are trade agreements," he says.

"We have historically traded with Asia. Our economy is transitioning from the mining investment boom phase to a more balanced economy with a heavy weighting on services. We are very good at that. If you are selling services you have to be where the customers are and that means building businesses and investing in the region."

While trade deals are opening doors, the reality is many Australian companies are reluctant to invest in a region where the risks are high and competition from increasingly savvy local players is rising.

A big part of the problem is that chief executives, like their investors and many politicians, are hostage to short-termism and forced to think in three- or four-year time horizons.

Building a business in Asia can take 10 to 15 years and is incredibly risky. One senior investment banker told Chanticleer this means most of the boards he deals with believe the risks of dealing with a culture they have little understanding of overshadow the potential financial rewards. Risk also depends where you want to do business. The World Bank ranks Singapore as the easiest country in the world to do business, while Myanmar ranks 167th.

One chief executive who went out on a limb to give Asia a shot was ANZ Banking Group's Mike Smith, whose super-regional strategy still divides the market, despite being the fact the bank is one of the few Australian financial institutions with a presence in the region.

Telstra chief Andy Penn, who has already had some luck in Asia when he ran insurance giant AXA, is trying to build a new mobile phone network in the highly competitive Philippine market.

One of the few recent Australian success stories in China is Blackmores, the Australian company that has made a fortune selling vitamins in Asia. It was one of the best performing stocks of the year. But companies like this are few and far between. It requires patience, which Blackmores boss Christine Holgate ranks as her top tip for doing business in the region.

"The first piece of advice that I'm not personally very good at is being patient. Don't assume that what you do in Australia and what's right for Australia is right for the market places up in Asia. Each country is very different. You need to invest in learning that marketplace. Hire a strong local team," Holgate told Chanticleer in an interview earlier this year.

Patience is the most common piece of advice for companies trying to break into Asia. The other is not to bite off more than you can chew.

"Any business going into China or India is moving into an enormous market. It is easy to get dazzled by the size of the market and the size of the opportunities. You cannot do business on that scale … you have to find your own niche and your own opportunities. That involves starting small, taking a long-term view and building your business over time," Richard Lancaster, the Australian-born chief executive of Hong Kong's CLP Group, told Chanticleer.

"As a foreigner as well you have to build a track record. You have to be seen to be there supporting the economy, supporting the country and building that reputation and that relationship over time.

Lancaster understands China better than many Australian executives. His company has prioritised investment in China, where it is investing in clean coal and renewable energy. But like many experts Chanticleer spoke to on the issue, he is worried that Australia's cultural isolation from the region remains a major impediment.

"Geographically, Australia is part of Asia but culturally and from a business mindset it has never fully embraced," he says.

"The trade agreements are certainly a step in the right direction. But what is critically important is understanding how to do business in Asia. It is taking the time and putting the effort into understanding the Asia way of doing business."

Australia has long had a reputation for failing to engage with Asia. Public comments by Turnbull suggests he knows this is important and has singled out opportunities in the region, particularly with China, as key reasons to be optimistic.

Minister for Foreign Affairs Julia Bishop's new Colombo plan has resurrected the student scholarship programs of the 1950s and helped restore links with the region.

Gillard's white paper had plenty of critics. It included aspirational goals and some of the policy suggestions lacked detail, but it did lay out a plan for taking things forward. The paper recommended one-third of Australian boards have Asian experience. That was always going to be a challenging target and the diversity debate around boards since then has focused on gender rather than on ethnic or age diversity.

Advocates for a long-term policy solution say the government will need to develop a national plan to help Australian companies capitalise on opportunities to sell local products or help with infrastructure investment in Asia. But it needs to happen fast.

Michael.smith@fairfaxmedia.com.au

Twitter: @MikeSmithAFR

Tony Boyd is on leave

HEADLINE: Thanks a little: reject prezzies a boon for Gumtree, eBay
INTRO: Cashing in Family and friends can miss the mark at Christmas.
TEXT:
Cashing in Family and friends can miss the mark at Christmas.

Ill-fitting clothes and fondue sets are among the most unwanted presents this Christmas, if a flood of listings to online marketplaces in anything to go by. Thousands of items have been put up for sale on Gumtree and eBay as their recipients look to cash in on an estimated $630 million worth of unwanted Christmas gifts.

But sellers should expect to lose, because the resale value for unwanted gifts can be as low as 50 per cent of the retail value. More than 8000 unwanted gifts are listed on Gumtree, including an iPhone 6S Plus for a dad who would prefer an iPhone 6s, a Star Wars R2D2 suitcase for a seller who is not a Star Wars fan, and even an unopened Secret Santa gift for a seller who has no faith in his family to give him the right Christmas gift.

"I'm not taking the risk and [am] offering the present to the world to open," the seller of the unopened Secret Santa present wrote on Gumtree.

eBay also has 400 items listed under the unwanted gift category, including a bra that was the wrong size for the seller and a pair of Nike shoes for a partner who wore them around the house for about half an hour before deciding he did not like them.

The website sent its users a message on Sunday offering the opportunity to sell up to three items free, asking users to "cash in on your Christmas extras and get the gift you really want".

Meanwhile, in the US, eBay has set up selling stations in three Westfield shopping centres to allow consumers to resell their unwanted gifts.

But most recipients looking to turn disappointment into cash find one thing in common: the trade in unwanted gifts is a buyer's market.

For example, $3000 La Mer moisturising cream has a Gumtree price tag of $1800, and $137 YSL perfume a price tag of $55.

NORA executive chairman and dealsdirect.com.au co-founder Paul Greenberg said sellers should be aware gifts lose value as soon as they are returned to the marketplace, and retailers should come up with a solution for consumers who may want the option to get their money back.

"You lose a percentage of the retail price the minute you return to the marketplace," he said. "The differential between retail price and brand new price is not that huge in some cases, but it is still a sting in the tail."

CHOICE's Matt Levey said most goods tended to lose value when resold in the second-hand market and consumers should consider getting gift exchange cards or even giving them cash. "If you want to give someone some flexibility to get the gift they want, give cash. Gift cards tend to lock people into a particular store and come with all sorts of unwanted issues," Mr Levey said.

Under consumer laws, consumers cannot get their money back simply because they do not like the product.

Gumtree's Kirsty Dunn said clothing, jewellery and fad kitchen appliances such as doughnut makers and fondue sets were among the most unwanted presents listed on the website.

"Clothing and jewellery are the most risky gifts, because unless you know them absolutely 100 per cent, it's likely it doesn't fit them or it isn't their style," Ms Dunn said. People used Gumtree to sell unwanted gifts so they can avoid uncomfortable conversations, she said.

"People don't want to have an awkward conversation with the gift giver, like, 'Have you got the receipt?' or 'I don't like the gift'."

She said it was common for sellers to list gifts that are given as a joke, such as a hairbrush for a bald guy.

A Galaxy survey commissioned by Gumtree found Australians waste $630 million a year buying undesirable Christmas gifts.

HEADLINE: No respite after world's hottest year
INTRO: As bushfires burned in Victoria and Western Australia and 2015 was expected to be the world's hottest year on record, weather forecasters could see little respite in the year ahead.
TEXT:
As bushfires burned in Victoria and Western Australia and 2015 was expected to be the world's hottest year on record, weather forecasters could see little respite in the year ahead.

Cities around Australia recorded temperatures well above average in the closing weeks of 2015, even as Australia as a whole fell short of is record average for a year, set in 2013 at 22.3 degrees, 1.2 degrees higher than the long-term average.

Depending on what happens in the last week of December, 2015 is forecast to be between the fourth- and sixth-hottest year on record at 22 degrees, says the Bureau of Meteorology.

Globally, 2015 is on track to be the warmest year on record and 2016 is likely to be at least as warm, if not warmer, according to the UK Met Office.

The global average temperature for 2016 is expected to be 14.8 degrees, which is 0.8 degrees above the long-term average.

"This forecast suggests that by the end of 2016 we will have seen three record, or near-record years in a row for global temperatures," Professor Adam Scaife at the UK Met Office said. The forecast takes into account man-made global warming as well as the effects of El Niño.

According to the UK Met Office, global warming, combined with smaller, natural fluctuations, is pushing the global climate to unprecedented levels of warmth.

Bureau of Meteorology climatologist Blair Trewin said he expected above-average temperatures in the first half of 2016 due to the influence of El Niño.

But when El Niño ends in autumn next year the temperature was likely to return to normal and rainfall would also return to normal levels, Mr Trewin said.

The official 2016 weather forecast for Australia will be released on January 6.

In the year to October the global average temperature was 14.7 degrees, 0.7 degrees above the long-term average.

According to Weatherzone, Adelaide is on track to have the hottest December in more than 100 years, at the average daytime temperature of 32.1 degrees, which is five degrees higher than the long-term average.

Canberra is also on track to have the hottest December in 75 years, at the average daytime temperature of 29.8 degrees compared with the long-term average of 26.2 degrees.

Sydney and Melbourne are also expecting a hot December, although not as hot as some of the other capital cities around Australia.

The average daytime temperature for Sydney in December is 26.5 degrees, which is one degree hotter than the usual, and for Melbourne, 27.1 degrees, which is three degrees hotter.

Meanwhile, Victoria remained on high alert for more bushfires after bushfires near the Great Ocean Road destroyed 103 homes on Christmas Day. Extreme temperatures were expected to continue through the end of the year, with temperatures in central and western Victoria forecast to reach the high 30s on New Year's Eve.

Extreme weather events have hit the UK this week with heavy flooding sweeping through northern England following weeks of rain. In much of Europe and east coast USA an unseasonably warm winter has seen record high average temperatures. In Switzerland that meant a green Christmas for many, with sleds being fitted with wheels in lieu of mountain snow.

HEADLINE: ANYONE FOR PETANQUE?
INTRO: The quintessentially French game has a small following in Australia but its popularity is growing - not least because you can hold a glass of wine in one hand and the boule in the other, writes Jonathan Barrett.
TEXT:
The quintessentially French game has a small following in Australia but its popularity is growing - not least because you can hold a glass of wine in one hand and the boule in the other, writes Jonathan Barrett.

Back in 1910, Provence cafe owner Ernest Pitiot looked at his chair-bound friend, Jules Lenoir, cheerlessly watch a game of boules. Lenoir's rheumatism was playing up, and the days had passed of him taking an energetic trot before throwing the ball, as was customary in the popular game of the day, jeu provençal. Pitiot puffed out his cheeks, exhaled, and came up with a new boules game his friend could play: the length of the pitch was halved and, most importantly, players could throw the ball from a stationary start, with pès tancats, or feet fixed. You could even sit down if you wanted to. Petanque would go on to become the dominant boules game in France.

Fast forward a little over a century, and 26 teams are competing in a local petanque tournament near a famous wine-growing region. But it is not rosé-producing Provence, in the south-east of France. This is the south-west of Western Australia, near Margaret River. A team from Mauritius is doing well, as are several teams consisting of a mix of Australians, European expats and French travellers.

A team of young French men, all in Australia on working holiday visas, tell me that playing petanque has been their weekend activity for as long as they can remember. "You start when you're young and you play until you're dead," says the dreadlocked Thomas Henry. The prize-money tournament is hosted by Whicher Ridge vineyard owners Neil and Cathy Howard in an unashamed bid to mix business and pleasure. Given it's one of the few sports where you can hold a glass of wine while you play, the vineyard setting is entirely appropriate, and more than a few competitors buy a few bottles of the vineyard's finest.

Petanque might have only a niche following in Australia, and is clearly overshadowed by lawn bowls, but its popularity is growing. Part of its appeal is clearly linked to the social element. "I come from a family of lawn bowlers, but it was never something that I really wanted to get into," one of the country's top over-60s players, Helen Bayet says. "[Petanque] was a lot more fun. If you can hold a boule in one hand and a glass of wine in the other, well, it's great."

Like lawn bowls, the aim of petanque is to get your boules as close to the jack as possible. Players stand in a small circle; this used to be drawn on the gravel-playing "piste", but is now more often marked by a plastic circle. At the end of each round, the team scores as many points as it has boules closer to the jack than the closest shot of their opponents.

The winning player or team - you can play singles, doubles or triples - is the first to reach 13 points. But games are also often timed, which means that if you are ahead when the time runs out, you win. This can lead to allegations of time wasting, especially if people are betting on the result, as is the case in parts of France.

"When there's a lot of betting going on, it gets competitive," Petanque Federation Australia president Joe Corcoran says. "There's time wasting, but there are other things you need to keep an eye on. People do things like step outside the edge of the circle to create a different angle. People do all sorts of things to help them score a point."

If this all sounds rather competitive for a social sport, that's because for many players it isn't strictly social. It could soon be an Olympic event. The sport's international federation is pushing for petanque to be included in the 2024 Olympics; an event France wants to host. Part of any bid to have a new sport included in the world's premier sporting event relies on proving it has widespread appeal outside its country of origin. It's unclear whether petanque will be included, but gaining supporters in Australia won't hurt its chances.

And while France's colonial past has ensured petanque is played in several places around the globe - former French colonies and protectorates like Tunisia and Algeria traditionally field strong teams at tournaments - the sport has taken off in the most unlikely of places.

The late Princess Srinagarindra of Thailand fell in love with petanque after living for a time in Switzerland. She promoted the sport in her homeland, and Thailand now boasts several world champions. Thai success seems to be rubbing off on its neighbours, with most of south-east Asia competitive in petanque tournaments around the world. The sport is said to improve co-ordination and aid strategic thinking. It can help develop nerves of steel - or destroy you.

On the advice of a petanque player, I recently watched a video of the 2006 World Championships, from Grenoble, France, between a French and Tunisian team. It's a bit like watching a sudden death golf play-off; the tension never ceases. As the pressure mounts, players shuffle the metals balls between their hands faster and faster, presumably to alleviate tension. When the crowd falls silent, the click, click, click of the metal balls becomes the predominant sound. It would not be out of place on an Alfred Hitchcock film soundtrack.

There are many reasons petanque might thrive in Australia and abroad and a few why it may not, according to Murdoch University professor and social scientist Toby Miller. He says some sports have natural barriers to expansion, for instance, AFL's requirement for a vast field. Ice hockey and golf are naturally inhibited. NFL is, of course, just strange to anyone not born in North America.

While petanque lacks certain athletic attributes, it does have a "low barrier to entry" as the equipment is cheap, the skill level required to play in a social game is low.

"But the difficult thing for petanque in Australia is to show it is a different form of game to one extremely familiar to us, lawn bowls," says Miller, who co-authored the book Globalisation and Sport.

There is a school of thought that says two similar sports will struggle to thrive in one jurisdiction as they tend to cannibalise one another. For example, cricket will dominate baseball or vice versa in any one country, given their similarities. When two similar sports do co-exist successfully, like Rugby Union and Rugby League, there is often a historical cultural or socioeconomic element, such as the two codes' "gentleman" and "working class" roots, respectively.

At risk of upsetting lawn bowlers, my view is that petanque could be more successful than bowls in attracting more diverse - and younger - players in Australia. The game is faster-paced than bowls, does not need a long bowling green to play on and includes the strangely satisfying "shooting" element, where you aggressively knock a rival's ball out of the way. While lawn bowlers "drive" with similar aggression, the shot is used less frequently.

And then petanque has that certain French chic the all-white-wearing lawn bowling organisations don't quite portray. In 2010, fashion labels Chanel and Louis Vuitton even released petanque sets in soft leather cases to celebrate the sport's centenary. I don't see any such sets at the laid-back Whicher Ridge event, where some players are wearing whimsical berets in a nod to the game's French origins.

A team from the Perth Petanque Club: John Rowe, Walter Lubtschenko and Mattias Laukart, won the tournament.

It seems petanque's best chance of enticing more lawn bowls turncoats and attracting a new generation of Australian players lies with its Olympics bid. The increased exposure and funding that comes with being an Olympic sport could catapult the sport onto the world stage in a way Ernest Pitiot could never have imagined when he came up with the boules game his chair-bound friend could play.

HEADLINE: Clarification
INTRO: The Pierpont column published on December 23 said that the RSPCA had investigated a complaint against a Broken Hill station where shearers were alleged to have been swearing at sheep. HEADLINE: Fundies get to the heart of social impact investing
INTRO: Raising money for charity has never been easy, but in the last nine months a group of fund managers has raised $1.64 million for children's causes.
TEXT:
Raising money for charity has never been easy, but in the last nine months a group of fund managers has raised $1.64 million for children's causes.

It's an impressive number, and Wilson Asset Management founder Geoff Wilson says if the model works, the group could contribute triple this amount within the next year.

And he expects the group to contribute more than $20 million a year within the next decade to charities aimed at helping children and people with mental health problems.

The initiative is a creative philanthropic twist on the funds management business model, which has traditionally charged for its services based on a percentage of funds under management. Wilson persuaded 33 highly regarded fund managers and a handful of administration and service providers to offer their services free.

He set up two ASX-listed investment companies and assured investors they could earn better than market index returns if they invested. The vehicles would take the obligatory 1 per cent that would otherwise be paid to the managers and donate that direct to chosen charities.

The Future Generation Investment Company invests in the domestic equities market and listed in September 2014 with $200 million, while the Future Generation Global Company invests in overseas equities and listed in September 2015 with $302.1 million.

The compounding effect is built into the model: the bigger the funds get, the more money they give away. Initial shareholders hold options that will be called on to raise additional capital at the end of the first year, which means if performance is good they're assured to grow.

In its first full year, Future Generations Investment Company returned 11.3 per cent, 3.2 per cent better than the ASX All Ordinaries Accumulation Index.

"It's clear it's up to private enterprise to step up in some of these areas, particularly where the issue might not be an area where government wins votes by focusing on," Wilson says.

Louise Walsh, who left her position as chief executive office of Philanthropy Australia at the end of last year to become co-CEO of Future Generations, says the government allocates half the amount it should to mental health, given the scale of the problem.

For Geoff Wilson, the seed to set up the charitable structure was planted when he was exposed to mental illness and children at risk while volunteering as a Lifeline counsellor as part of a company initiative.

The result was possibly the most tangible outcome of a social impact investing initiative in Australia in 2015.

Social and affordable housing is an obvious area where private money will be put to work to solve shortfalls in government funding, says Richard Brandweiner, chief investment officer of First State Super.

Brandweiner and four of his contemporaries, including Cbus investment manager of public markets Brett Chatfield, have formed an informal working group to discuss with government ways to invest in areas such as social housing.

If superannuation money finds its way into such projects, there would not be any compromise on investment returns, Brandweiner emphasises.

"Coming up with ways to deploy capital that meets traditional fiduciary tests while making a huge difference to society is an exciting prospect," he says.

Progress towards this goal looks good. The NSW government launched two social benefit bonds in 2013.

The Newpin social benefit bond, developed in partnership with UnitingCare Burnside and Social Ventures Australia, raised $7 million to help safely restore children to their families and prevent children from entering out-of-home care. The Benevolent Society Bond, with The Benevolent Society, Westpac and Commonwealth Bank, raised $10 million for the Resilient Families Service to work intensively with families to improve relationships and parenting, and prevent children from entering out-of-home care.

Meanwhile, the NSW government created Australia's first social impact investing policy, which highlights 10 actions to deliver more social impact investing actions and remove barriers for investment.

HEADLINE: Party's over but headache may last a bit
INTRO: The Australian housing market is on track for a bad hangover in 2016. After a year of partying at double-digit price growth, particularly for Sydney and Melbourne, the two main markets are set to cool, experts say.
TEXT:
The Australian housing market is on track for a bad hangover in 2016. After a year of partying at double-digit price growth, particularly for Sydney and Melbourne, the two main markets are set to cool, experts say.

Even the markets that were doing it tough in 2015 - Perth, Darwin and Canberra - will not be getting a reprieve. The threat of an economic downturn is not out of the question, which could further dent softening markets.

But it is not all bad, particularly for Sydney and Melbourne buyers, who will relish a "welcome cooling off period", Aussie Home Loans chairman John Symond says.

"Next year should provide buyers with a bit more breathing space to relax and take their time choosing the best house or apartment for their needs and aspirations," he says.

Sydney and Melbourne closed the year with growth of 12.8 per cent and 11.8 per cent respectively, according to Corelogic RP Data.

Those numbers will be replaced by 3 per cent and 1 per cent in 2016, head of research Tim Lawless says.

"Over the past three months we saw five of the eight capital cities record a decline in dwelling values, with Sydney down 1 per cent and Melbourne, 0.5 per cent," he says. "We may see further declines during 2016; however, considering the high rate of population growth and stronger economic conditions in these cities, I'd be surprised if the fall was more than 5 per cent before conditions start to level."

"The significant house price growth disparities between capital cities is set to converge though 2016," Domain chief economist Andrew Wilson says.

Melbourne and Brisbane will overtake Sydney in the growth stakes, many experts conclude.

"I'm not sure where the notion of a significant slowdown in the Melbourne housing market is coming from, but the data to date is completely contrary to this notion," SQM Research managing director Louis Christopher says.

Victorian Planning Minister Richard Wynne just approved one of the largest single development proposals for Melbourne - Malaysian developer PJ Development's $1.5 billion six-tower project at Southbank.

But Brisbane and south-east Queensland could still outperform Melbourne. McGrath Ltd's John McGrath swears by the region, as does Brisbane luxury agent Johnston Dixon's John Johnston.

"Putting all of the psychological and economic factors at play, south-east Queensland is probably either already at or near the bottom of the current downturn; when you're at the bottom, the only way is up," Johnston says.

"Yields in Brisbane are much higher compared with Sydney and Melbourne ... and affordability is far superior to the two larger cities," Lawless adds.

Hobart is another one to watch. The highest rental yields can now be found in Hobart and Darwin, both averaging 5.4 per cent, according to Corelogic RP Data. However while Hobart yields are rising, the same cannot be said for Darwin, where rents are falling.

Christopher says it is fast becoming Australia's most undervalued city.

Perth and Darwin will not recover well - there are no signs of bottoming for Perth's falling housing prices. Canberra's oversupplied housing market will stall, as will Adelaide's.

"Adelaide is not in any type of dire shape like Perth and Darwin, but nothing to write home about either."

Laing+Simmons managing director Leanne Pilkington warns that property agents will be tested, but first-home buyers will see opportunities.

"If the door is closing somewhat to investors, another may open for first-home buyers; supply is up and the price heat has subsided,"

But the key tests in 2016 will be the national and global economies, and policy changes. Symond says 2016 will feature global uncertainty and slow economic growth.

Sydney

"Specifically, I see opportunities in Wollongong as well as the Central Coast. Their proximity to Sydney combined with the significant value gap will be very attractive to metropolitan buyers."

John McGrath, McGrath Limited

"We're expecting infrastructure improvements will prove great news for suburbs such as Wentworth Falls, Leura and in Katoomba, with prices expected to grow by 5 to 10 per cent once again in 2016. Also, the state government's recent announcement that work will start on new metro stations at Crows Nest, North Sydney, Barangaroo, Pitt Street and Waterloo in 2018 had an almost immediate impact on property values."Angus Raine, Raine & Horne

Melbourne

"All round Melbourne Vicroads has imposed speed cuts from 60 km/h to 40, 100 km/h to 80. What that's doing is putting pressure on commuting time and creating congestion. The places to invest are within 10 kilometres of the CBD. It's a no-brainer: Port Melbourne, St Kilda East and possibly Williamstown, Altona. On the north side,North Melbourne, Flemington, Ascot Vale." John Bongiorno, Marshall White

"It's the regional towns such as Sunbury and Gisborne that are expected to continue to perform solidly in 2016 - not strictly investment plays but their value can be linked to the fact they are part of Victoria's subdivision belt." Randolph Clements, Raine & Horne

Brisbane

"The Gold Coast will continue to be a hotspot in 2016 thanks to the additional infrastructure and business confidence generated by the city's decision to host the 2018 Commonwealth Games. Closer to Brisbane, the housing market in inner city Woolloongabba will attract attention in 2016." Angus Raine, Raine & Horne

"I nominate the Brisbane suburban markets of Woolloongabba, Paddington, Teneriffe and Lutwyche as ones that are primed for future growth for a variety of micro to macroeconomic reasons." Neil Smoli, Aviate Group

Perth

"Buyers looking to get into upmarket, well-established suburbs like Subiaco could use the current market weakness. There's more properties for sale there than buyers. Beachside Cottesloe and suburbs near the city like Shenton Park and Subiaco might now be affordable for people previously priced out." Nigel Satterley, Satterley Property Group

"Buyers were entering the "western suburbs mortgage belt" through purchases in pricey suburbs like Peppermint Grove." Gavin Hegney, Hegney Property Group

Adelaide

"The north-western areas of Magill and Rostrevor are worth looking at. Both have had 10-20 per cent growth in the last 12 months, and still plenty in the tank. Campbelltown council has also rezoned some land." Phil Harris, Harris Real Estate

"The state government's investment in the Darlington exchange will encourage more buyers and investors. Beachside suburbs such as O'Sullivan Beach and Christies Beach will be on the radar." Michael McDonald, Raine & Horne

Hobart and Darwin

Hobart: "New Town, an inner northern suburb of Hobart, is sure to be a winner with savvy investors. A gross yield which is a tick under 5 per cent and the prospect of some long-term growth will make Newtown a Tasmanian suburb to watch in 2016." Ron Brooks, Raine & Horne

Darwin: "Darwin is a relatively small capital city property market - therefore it will return to form relatively swiftly in 2016 as more interstate buyers start to make their presence felt." Angus Raine

HEADLINE: Bank curbs won't deter Chinese buyers
INTRO: ANZ is making it harder for overseas buyers to get loans but the move is unlikely to curb Chinese interest in Australian property in 2016, property experts and banks say.
TEXT:
ANZ is making it harder for overseas buyers to get loans but the move is unlikely to curb Chinese interest in Australian property in 2016, property experts and banks say.

ANZ is clamping down on overseas buyers with temporary visas who want to buy residential and investment properties.

But Chinese property marketer Juwai.com expects Chinese investment into Australian residential property to "set new records between now and 2020".

"It's foolhardy right now to make a firm short-term prediction, because too much is happening and any single event internationally could create a boom or reversal in any given quarter," Juwai.com co-founder Simon Henry said.

"But we are very optimistic for 2016 and even more so for the remaining portion of this decade.

"Our 2020 forecast for all Chinese international real estate investment, not just residential, is for $220 billion, which would be up more than fourfold from $52 billion in 2014."

However, a decline in bank lending to investors and capital controls imposed in China might slow investments in the short term.

ANZ's move follows earlier lending changes imposed by all the big banks, such as lifting the amounts a buyer must have as a deposit, aimed at curbing riskier overseas buying.

"We are continuing to review our portfolio," an ANZ spokesman said in a statement sent to mortgage brokers.

"This is to ensure we respond to current market dynamics and align with regulator guidelines."

The latest changes are targeting borrowers with temporary, or provisional visas, which can lead to the grant of a permanent visa. They allow the holder to stay in Australia for longer than 12 months.

Under the new restrictions the maximum loan-to-value ratio - a measure of the loan to the value of the asset being bought - has been reduced from 80 per cent to 70 per cent.

The bank has also increased the range of products for which temporary, or provisional visa holders, will not be eligible.

Products still available include the fixed and standard variable home and residential investment loans.

The bank has told brokers that discretionary pricing might be available if there is "competitive justification for the request".

Brokers say the latest changes are targeting the Chinese market, which has been spending billions of dollars on Australian residential property, particularly in Melbourne and Sydney.

Other measures have included reducing interest rate discounts, raising rate "sensitivity buffers" and ruling out some income, such as bonuses, when assessing an applicant's ability to repay a loan.

Juwai.com hopes the end of the current Chinese capital controls, which it sees as temporary, will lead to more capital flowing into Australia.

"When they do cut back on the capital controls, a complete removal would deliver an extra estimated $75.7 billion to Australia's residential real estate markets," Mr Henry said.

HEADLINE: Where the jobs will be in 2016
INTRO: The healthcare, technology, construction and education sectors offer the best hopes for jobseekers in 2016, in what is expected to be a stronger year than 2015, recruiters say.
TEXT:
The healthcare, technology, construction and education sectors offer the best hopes for jobseekers in 2016, in what is expected to be a stronger year than 2015, recruiters say.

Hays Australia and New Zealand managing director Nick Deligiannis said while it would continue to be an employers' market, with the number of job seekers outstripping roles, there would be a slight "rebalancing". "Where there is an undersupply, employees will be in a good position and can expect multiple job offers," he said.

Mr Deligiannis expects more jobs in the healthcare sector, with demand for professionals increasing and companies having to look at different ways to attract workers, especially to regional and remote areas. "It's a pretty active sector, spurred on with the ageing population, national disability insurance scheme and the creation of new facilities," he said.

Jobs in technology will also continue to grow, Mr Deligiannis said, with roles analysing big data in high demand.

He expects to see increased demand in the finance sector for specialised roles in business and commerce analytics. "Compliance and risk management roles will not decrease and organisations will keep investing in these areas," he said.

The overall jobs market is more positive than the same time last year, according to Randstad market analyst Steve Shepherd. "No area is particularly underperforming."

Mr Shepherd said he expected the construction and education sectors to be the areas to watch in 2016. "The construction industry had a strong second half in 2015 and there will be more demand for white collar workers such as estimators, project managers and architects, especially in the civil sector, driven by infrastructure projects," he said. "Melbourne and Sydney will be the dominant markets. The competition for talent is heating up."

Mr Shepherd said free-trade agreements and a weaker Australian dollar were helping the education sector, with demand beating expectations in the fourth quarter of 2015. "There's been a significant increase in the number of roles on offer year on year. But this [sector] is the potential star of future jobs growth in Australia."

However, Mr Shepherd said apart from wealth management - superannuation and financial planning - the finance sector was, and would remain, relatively flat. He said the retail and hospitality sectors were "ones to watch".
